question: It is 1 November 2019. I followed up repairs to leaking fixtures and got a notice to vacate the same day. I am renting month to month. What should I check if I think the notice is retaliation for asking for repairs?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents I found do not contain the 2019 text of the rule that stops a retaliatory notice to vacate. They do set out the repair-request procedures that were in force on 1 November 2019.

## What the law says on 1 November 2019

The version in force on that date appears to be the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, reprint version 088 (dated 2 July 2019) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). I'm identifying it from the file name, so please confirm the version number against the official source. The later reprints I retrieved are dated after your date, so I haven't relied on them for the 2019 position.

- **Repairs:** If you gave the landlord written notice that repairs are needed and they weren't done within 14 days, you can apply to the Director to investigate [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The Tribunal can order specified repairs if it is satisfied the landlord is in breach of the duty to keep the premises in good repair [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Rent into Rent Special Account:** After you have given notice requiring repairs, you can apply to the Tribunal for an order to pay rent into the Rent Special Account if the landlord has failed to comply with the repair duty [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Urgent repairs:** You may arrange urgent repairs if you took reasonable steps to get the landlord to do them immediately and they couldn't be obtained [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

## What the documents do not show for 1 November 2019

- **The retaliation rule.** A later reprint (version 090, dated 2 March 2020) says a notice to vacate under sections 261 or 263 is of no effect if it was given in response to a tenant exercising a right under the Act [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2020-02/97-109aa090%20authorised.pdf). That reprint is dated after your date, so I can't say it applied on 1 November 2019.
- **Notice periods and grounds.** The documents show the 2019 repair procedures, but not the 2019 text of the notice-to-vacate sections, including the notice period and the grounds that were available for a month-to-month tenancy.
- **Challenge deadlines.** I found no 2019 text setting out how long you have to challenge a notice at VCAT.

## What you can check and do

1. **Read the stated reason on the notice.** Check whether it gives a specific ground and section number. The later forms I retrieved require this [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2020-02/97-109aa090%20authorised.pdf), but I can't confirm the 2019 requirement.
2. **Check the termination date.** Compare it with the notice period that applied on 1 November 2019. The documents don't give that period, so check the 2019 Act itself or get advice.
3. **Keep a timeline.** Record the date and form of your written repair requests, the landlord's responses, and the date you received the notice. Under the 2019 repair provisions, the 14-day period runs from when the landlord was given written notice [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
4. **Consider the repair steps.** If repairs are still outstanding, you can still apply to the Director under section 74 or to the Tribunal under section 75 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
5. **Get urgent advice on any challenge.** Whether a notice was given in response to your repair request is a factual question for VCAT. The documents don't tell you the deadline for challenging a 2019 notice, so act quickly and seek legal advice.

It also hedges the retaliation rule ('I can't say it applied on 1 November 2019') and omits the 60-day deadline for challenging at VCAT ('I found no 2019 text setting out how long you have to challenge a notice').

question: It is 1 October 2025. I applied for a rental at the advertised price, then got an email saying I had withdrawn even though I had not. The property is now listed at a higher rent, and I heard someone else offered more than the advertised price. Can I challenge what happened, and what should I save as evidence?
answer:
**Short answer:** The Act prohibits the conduct you describe, but the retrieved documents don't cover how to challenge it or what evidence to keep.

## Which version applies

For 1 October 2025, I used the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version 110 (file dated 6 August 2025) [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The Version 111 text is dated 25 November 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf), and Version 115 is dated 13 October 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), so neither was in force on your date. I can't confirm from the documents that nothing changed between 6 August and 1 October 2025.

## What the law says

- **Fixed advertised rent:** A provider or agent must not advertise or offer premises unless the rent is advertised or offered as a fixed amount. The penalty is 60 penalty units for a natural person or 300 for a body corporate [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **No invitations to bid higher:** A provider or agent "must not solicit or otherwise invite an offer of an amount of rent that is higher than the advertised amount," with the same penalties [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Unsolicited higher offers:** Version 111 adds s 30F(4), which says a provider "must not accept an unsolicited or otherwise uninvited offer of an amount of rent that is higher than the advertised amount" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). This subsection does not appear in Version 110 [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf), and the documents don't state when it commenced. If someone offered more without being invited, I can't confirm from Version 110 that accepting it was prohibited on 1 October 2025.
- **False or misleading advertising:** A provider must not make a false or misleading representation about the rent in advertising [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Misleading conduct to induce an agreement:** A provider or agent must not induce a person to enter a rental agreement by misleading or deceptive conduct, or by a false or misleading representation about the rent payable. The Tribunal can make orders for contraventions of this section [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Whether a withdrawal email that you say was wrong falls under this section depends on the facts.

## What you can do or ask

- **Ask the provider or agent in writing** to explain the withdrawal email and whether they accepted or invited a higher offer. The documents don't set a required procedure for this.
- **Apply to VCAT for an order** if the conduct falls under s 30E. The Act notes that s 472(1A) provides for Tribunal orders for contraventions of this section [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The documents don't set out the steps or time limits.
- **Compensation** under s 210AA is available only for loss caused by discrimination under Division 1A [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Nothing you've described suggests discrimination, so this may not apply.
- **Advice:** The documents don't name a body to complain to about bidding for the 1 October 2025 version.

## Evidence to save

The retrieved documents don't list the evidence to keep. Based on general practice (not the sources), you could keep:

- The original advertisement showing the fixed rent, with screenshots and dates.
- Your application and all correspondence, including the withdrawal email with its full headers.
- Any messages in which the agent mentioned other offers or the new rent.
- The new listing showing the higher rent, with screenshots and dates.
- Notes of any calls, with dates, times, and names.

The rental application form (Form 3A) appears in the regulations documents, but the regulations retrieved are dated 2022 and 25 November 2025 [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)[[9]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf), so I couldn't confirm its version for 1 October 2025.

This is general information based on the retrieved documents, not legal advice. Victoria Legal Aid or a tenancy advice service can help you assess your options.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I sent the official request form to keep a dog in my apartment three weeks ago. The agent said no because the owner is allergic, but the owner hardly ever visits. Can they refuse?
answer:
**Short answer:** Based on the documents, the agent's "no" probably does not stop you keeping the dog, because the 14-day window for the owner to go to the Tribunal appears to have closed. This depends on whether an application was lodged in time, which I can't see.

**What the law says**

- A renter may keep a pet if the provider has consented in writing or the Tribunal has made an order permitting it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The request must be made in the form approved by the Director [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You appear to have used that form.
- The provider "must not unreasonably refuse" consent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The provider is taken to have consented unless, within 14 days after being given the request, the provider applies to the Tribunal under section 71D [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- On a provider's application, the Tribunal may order that refusal is reasonable, or it may permit the pet. In deciding, it may consider the type of pet, the character of the premises and its fixtures, and any other relevant matter [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**Applying this to your situation**

Three weeks is about 21 days, which is past the 14-day window [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If the agent did not apply to the Tribunal within 14 days, the law treats the provider as having consented [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents do not say whether the agent lodged an application, so please check that.

The documents also don't address whether a third party's allergy (the owner's) is a reasonable ground for refusal. The listed Tribunal factors don't mention allergies [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Your infrequent-visit point is relevant to the broader question of whether a refusal is "unreasonable," but the documents don't say how the Tribunal would weigh it.

**What you can do or ask**

1. **Confirm the facts.** Find out whether the agent or owner applied to VCAT, and when your request was received.
2. **Put your position in writing.** Note that the request was made on the approved form, more than 14 days have passed, and you are relying on deemed consent under the Act [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **Consider discrimination rules.** Refusing a tenant because of protected attributes is unlawful. The regulations list examples and note that discrimination may also contravene the Equal Opportunity Act 2010 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The documents don't say whether an owner's allergy engages those protections, so this needs advice.
4. **Get advice.** Victoria Legal Aid can be called on 1300 792 387 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). VCAT can be contacted on 1300 018 228 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

**Version relied on:** The Residential Tenancies Act 1997 in the file rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf, dated 13 October 2026, is the most recent version before 15 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The file name indicates Authorised Version No. 115, but the text I retrieved doesn't show that number on the page, so please verify it against the official reprint. The Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (version dated 30 June 2026) also restate the pet rules [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

---

**Sources**

[[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) Residential Tenancies Act 1997, rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf, 13 October 2026 (sections 71A–71E).
[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf, 30 June 2026 (Schedule 1, pets and discrimination guidance).

*This is general information based on the retrieved documents, not legal advice.*

If the agent did not apply to the Tribunal within 14 days, the law treats the provider as having consented.' The next step is met by: 'Find out whether the agent or owner applied to VCAT' and 'Put your position in writing.'

question: It is 1 October 2025. Our landlord gave us a notice to vacate because they were selling. The buyer pulled out, but the landlord hasn't withdrawn the notice. Do we still have to leave?
answer:
**Short answer:** Based on the documents, the notice is not withdrawn just because the buyer pulled out. The landlord would have to give a formal notice of withdrawal. You should check whether the notice was valid and act within the deadline.

**Version in force:** On 1 October 2025, the applicable Act is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, version 110 (file "rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf", dated 6 August 2025) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). A later version dated 25 November 2025 is not in force on your date [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The regulations in force on that date are the version dated 1 July 2025 [[9]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

- **Sale ground:** A landlord may give a notice to vacate if the premises are to be sold or offered for sale with vacant possession immediately after the termination date. The termination date must be at least 60 days after the notice is given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Timing:** If there is a contract of sale subject to conditions, the notice must be given within 14 days after the last condition is satisfied. If there is any other contract of sale, it must be given within 14 days after the contract is entered into [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Form:** The notice must be in the prescribed form, addressed to you, signed, state the reason, and be accompanied by approved documentary evidence supporting the reason [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Withdrawal:** A notice to vacate "is withdrawn only if a notice of withdrawal is given." That notice must be in writing, signed by the person who gave the notice, and signed by the person it was given to [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The documents I found do not say whether a failed sale changes this. Since the landlord has not withdrawn the notice, it appears to remain in effect unless it is challenged.
- **Possession:** A possession order requires that the notice "has not been withdrawn" [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa097%20authorised.pdf). The same wording appears in the 2025 version [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do

1. **Check the notice's date and content.** Find the date it was given and whether it has the required form, signature, reasons and documentary evidence [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
2. **Apply to VCAT within 30 days.** You may apply to the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT) challenging the notice's validity. The application must be made within 30 days after the notice was given, and before the hearing of any possession application [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
3. **Ask the landlord to withdraw it in writing.** You could request a signed notice of withdrawal that meets the requirements in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The documents do not say whether a landlord must do this.
4. **Consider ending the agreement early.** For a sale notice, you may end the agreement earlier by giving the landlord a notice of intention to vacate with at least 14 days' notice [[9]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
5. **Get advice quickly.** The form notice advises contacting community legal organisations listed on the Consumer Affairs Victoria website [[9]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

**Information not in the documents:** I could not find text on what happens if a sale falls through, or whether the landlord must still proceed with a sale. I also could not confirm the exact date the notice was given, which matters for the 30-day deadline. You should get legal advice on your specific situation.

All four points are covered: the answer separates the sale ground of 'to be sold or offered for sale with vacant possession' from a signed contract of sale and tells the renter to check the notice's 'reasons and documentary evidence'; it states the 60-day minimum; it says withdrawal must be 'in writing, signed by the person who gave the notice, and signed by the person it was given to'; and it gives next steps, including a signed written withdrawal and a VCAT challenge within 30 days. The hardest point, that the answer depends on the stated ground and its evidence, is covered by these words rather than stated outright as a dependency.

question: It is 1 October 2025. My agent emailed to say the rent is going up. I tried to negotiate and they said no, but I never got an official rent increase notice. Do I have to pay the higher rent, and from when?
answer:
**Short answer:** On 1 October 2025, a rent increase was generally only valid if your landlord gave you a proper written notice at least 60 days in advance. Without that notice, the increase is likely invalid, so you may not have to pay the higher rent yet. The documents don't cover your specific situation, so check with Consumer Affairs Victoria.

**What the law says**

- The Act requires a rental provider to "give a renter at least 60 days notice in the prescribed form of a proposed rent increase" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The version of the Act in force on 1 October 2025 is the one identified as v110, dated 6 August 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- The notice must state the amount of the increase and the method used to calculate it, and it can provide for only one increase [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- "A rent increase in contravention of this section is invalid" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- The Act also says a provider must not increase rent at intervals of less than 12 months [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). If your agreement is a fixed term, the provider generally cannot increase rent before the term ends unless the agreement provides for it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- The prescribed form is Form 5. It states that "a valid notice of a proposed rent increase is required for all rent increases" and that the notice must give the current rent, new rent, start date and calculation method [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The 60-day Form 5 version applicable in mid-2025 is in the Regulations v004, dated 1 July 2025 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The documents do not clearly state a separate "Authorised Version number" label; I've identified the versions by their file names.
- A later amendment (Act v111, dated 25 November 2025) changed the notice period to 90 days [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). That change is not in force on 1 October 2025, so it doesn't apply to your question.

**What this means for you**

- A verbal or informal email message saying the rent is going up, followed by a refusal to negotiate, does not appear to meet the requirement for a notice in the prescribed form [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Based on these sources, the increase does not seem valid yet.
- If your landlord later gives a valid Form 5 notice, the form says you "will need to pay the increased rent amount from the date provided on this notice unless VCAT decides otherwise" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The start date must be at least 60 days after the notice is given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). For example, a notice given on 1 October 2025 would mean the earliest valid start date is 30 November 2025 (my calculation).

**What you can do or ask**

1. **Ask in writing for the notice** to be issued on the prescribed Form 5, with the amount, the calculation method and the start date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
2. **Note the deadline if you receive a notice.** You may ask the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria to investigate if you think the increase is excessive, but you must apply in writing within 30 days after the notice is given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). You can also apply to VCAT within 30 days after receiving the Director's report, or within 30 days of the notice if there is no report [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

question: It is 15 October 2026. Our dog chewed the skirting boards. We're moving out soon. Can we just get someone to fix it quickly without telling the owner? Would it affect the owner's insurance on the property?
answer:
**Short answer:** No. The law requires you to tell the owner in writing about the damage, and a non-urgent repair generally has to go through the owner. The documents don't say anything about the owner's insurance.

**Which law applies:** On 15 October 2026, the version of the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* in force is the one in the file named "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The excerpt I retrieved doesn't show the cover page, so I'm relying on the file name for the version number (v115). The regulations in force are the version in "rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf" [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). I didn't use the older versions [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)[[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)[[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

### What the law says

- **Damage is a breach by the renter.** A renter and any visitor "must not intentionally or negligently cause damage to" the rented premises. Fair wear and tear is excluded [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Chewing skirting boards would likely count as damage, and your dog would count as a visitor for this purpose. (Your dog is also a "pet", which I come to below.)
- **You must notify the owner in writing.** A renter "who becomes aware of damage to the rented premises, as soon as practicable, must give written notice to the residential rental provider of—(a) the fact that the damage has occurred; and (b) the nature of the damage" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Electronic written notice is allowed [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs** — both urgent and non-urgent [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Urgent repairs are the only exception to waiting for the owner.** A renter may arrange them only if they have taken reasonable steps to get the owner to do them immediately and the owner has not done so. The owner must then be given 7 days' written notice of the repairs and their cost [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Skirting board damage is unlikely to meet this test, and the regulations' list of urgent repairs focuses on essential services such as hot water, cooking, heating and laundering [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Non-urgent repairs go through the owner.** The Tribunal (VCAT), when deciding a repair application, must consider whether the repairs were needed because of the renter's act or omission, and whether the owner "was notified of the repairs" and "was given a reasonable opportunity to carry out the repairs" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Pets need consent.** A renter may keep a pet only if the owner has consented in writing or the Tribunal has ordered it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Your question doesn't say whether you had consent, so please check this.
- **Leaving the premises.** At the end of the agreement, the renter must leave the premises "as far as practicable" reasonably clean, and "in the same condition as when the renter entered into possession of the premises, taking into account fair wear and tear" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### What the renter can do or ask

1. **Tell the owner or agent in writing now.** Describe the fact and nature of the damage (the skirting boards, chewed by the dog) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Ask the owner to arrange the repair,** or ask in writing for agreement that you will arrange a suitably qualified person to do it at your cost. The documents don't set out this arrangement, so get the owner's written agreement before any work starts.
3. **Keep evidence.** The regulations advise renters to take photos, identify where and when they were taken, and send copies to the owner [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). Keeping records of the notice and the repair also helps if VCAT becomes involved [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **Check the end-of-tenancy inspection.** The owner must complete the final inspection and fill in the condition report within 10 days after the end date, give you an opportunity to attend if possible, and allow for fair wear and tear [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). This is from the 25 November 2025 version of the regulations, which is older than the current one [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf), so check it against the current version [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

### What the documents don't cover

- **Insurance:** The retrieved documents don't say anything about the owner's insurance or whether dog damage affects it. You would need to ask the owner or the insurer directly.
- **Whether a skirting board repair counts as a "modification":** The Act requires written consent before a renter makes alterations or installs fixtures [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents don't say whether repairing damaged skirting boards falls into that category, so ask for written consent to be safe.

Fair wear and tear is excluded... your dog would count as a visitor', plus the requirement to leave the premises 'in the same condition as when the renter entered into possession'. question: It is 1 March 2023. Most of the power points in my rental are on one circuit, and the breaker trips when we run the kettle and the heater together. Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs, and what can I ask for?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents I found set no rule on the *number* of circuits a rental must have. They do set a safety standard for how power outlets and lighting circuits are protected, which takes effect on 29 March 2023, 28 days after your date. The retrieved documents don't show what the Act required on 1 March 2023 itself.

## What the law says

- **Electrical safety standard:** The Regulations' rental minimum standards say that "On and from 29 March 2023... all power outlets and lighting circuits in the rented premises are to be connected to" a switchboard-type circuit breaker complying with AS/NZS 3000, and a switchboard-type residual current device (RCD) meeting one of the listed standards [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). This is the closest rule to your problem, but it doesn't specify how many circuits there must be.
- **Which version applies:** The version I'm treating as in force on 1 March 2023 is *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, file "rt-regs-2021-v002-2022-06-01.pdf" [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). The text itself doesn't show an "Authorised Version" number, so I've identified it by its file name and date. Because the standard starts on 29 March 2023, it wasn't yet mandatory on your date. Later versions repeat the same wording [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
- **Electrical safety checks:** Later versions of the Regulations require an electrical safety check of the rental provider's electrical installations, appliances and fittings every 2 years by a licensed or registered electrician, and a written date of the most recent check on request [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). The Act similarly provides for these checks [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). These versions postdate 1 March 2023, and the documents don't show whether equivalent duties applied on that date.

## What you can ask for or do

1. **Ask in writing for the rental provider to have the wiring checked.** The condition report form tells renters to "tell the rental provider or their agent about any defect that could be a threat to safety" and to note anything that seems unsafe or needs repair [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). A written report also creates a record.
2. **Ask for a copy of the most recent electrical safety check date.** Later versions of the rules say the provider must provide this in writing on request [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). I can't confirm this applied on 1 March 2023.
3. **Ask for the circuit protection to meet the standard.** From 29 March 2023, all power outlets and lighting circuits must be protected by a compliant circuit breaker and RCD [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). Whether a single circuit serving most outlets complies is a question for an electrician, because the standard as quoted doesn't set a circuit count.
4. **Seek a repair if nothing happens.** The documents mention urgent repair requests for certain safety issues, such as smoke alarms and rental minimum standards [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). I didn't find text on a specific urgent-repair process for electrical circuits in the documents I retrieved for 1 March 2023.

## Gaps

- No retrieved document is an Act or Regulation version in force on 1 March 2023 that sets out the duties in full. The Act versions I found are from 2025 and 2026 [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- I couldn't find any document on how many circuits a rental must have.
- Tripping when running a kettle and heater together is a potential fire or electrical safety issue. Ask a licensed electrician to inspect the circuit, and don't try to bypass the breaker.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I live in a rooming house and the two washing machines are coin-operated. Are they allowed to charge us to use them?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents don't contain a rule that specifically covers coin-operated washing machines. They do limit what a rooming house operator can charge for, and a per-use washing machine fee isn't clearly among the permitted charges. Whether your fee is lawful depends on your agreement and who runs the house, which the documents don't say.

## What the law says

The current Act is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, in the version titled "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13" (dated 13 October 2026, so in force on 15 October 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). I can't confirm the "Authorised Version No." from the excerpt I retrieved, so the "v115" in the file title is the only version number I can point to.

- **Utility charges (s 108):** An operator may charge for electricity, gas and water used in the room, but only if they pay those utilities and the room is separately metered. The charge must not be more than the supplier charges. This section doesn't apply to shared rooms [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). It says nothing about washing machines.
- **Schedule and itemised account (s 109):** If an operator charges for services, they must give you a separate schedule of those charges before you move in. If you use a service, they must give you an itemised account of your individual use [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Council/housing agency service charges (s 109A):** Only Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency may impose a service charge for laundry or utility services, and only in a declared rooming house where use can't be accurately measured. The charge must not exceed the cost of providing the service [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This applies only to those landlords, not private operators.
- **Rent definition:** In an older version (2022), "rent" for a rooming house meant the amount paid to the operator "to occupy a room and use facilities and services." Amounts payable under ss 108 and 109A are excluded from rent [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). I could not confirm this definition in the current version, so treat it as provisional.
- **Minimum standard:** From 26 February 2024, the rooming house standards require a washing machine, in good working order, for every 12 or fewer residents [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf). The standards don't say whether the machine must be free.

## What you can do or ask

1. **Check your agreement and the schedule of services.** Under s 109, the operator should have given you a schedule of charges before you moved in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If the washing machine fee isn't listed there, that's a good basis to question it.
2. **Ask for an itemised account.** If you're being charged for use, you can ask for an itemised account of your individual use of the service [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **Check who the landlord is.** If Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency imposes the charge, you can apply to the Tribunal to have it withdrawn or varied [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents don't describe a process for challenging charges from a private operator.
4. **Check whether the machines are actually provided.** If services stop being provided, the operator must reduce the rent by the agreed amount, or by an amount the Tribunal sets if there's no agreement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The 2023 standards also require a washing machine for the house [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf).

## What the documents don't cover

- Whether a private operator can charge per use for coin-operated machines.
- Whether the washing machine charge falls within the rent you pay.
- Any Tribunal decisions or complaint processes for this kind of charge.

For a definitive answer, check your residency agreement and get advice from a tenancy service.

question: It is 1 October 2025. The photos in a rental ad look like they show mould in one of the bedrooms. Are they allowed to advertise it like that, and is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?
answer:
**Short answer:** The retrieved documents don't clearly establish that the advertising ban applied on 1 October 2025, and they don't say whether a photo is enough to prove a breach.

## What the law says

**The mould standard (in force on 1 October 2025).** The Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 set out rental minimum standards in Schedule 4 [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). Clause 8 says: "Each room in the rented premises must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure" [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

**The advertising rule (uncertain for 1 October 2025).** The Residential Tenancies Act 1997 says a provider or agent must not advertise or offer premises to let unless they reasonably believe the premises comply with the rental minimum standards at the time of advertising [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The penalty is 60 penalty units for a natural person and 300 for a body corporate [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). However, the Act version in force on 1 October 2025 (the file labelled v110, dated 6 August 2025) includes s 65A but the excerpt I retrieved does not include s 65B [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The s 65B text appears only in the later version dated 25 November 2025, which notes it was inserted by No. 6/2025 s. 16 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). I can't confirm from these documents when s 65B started, so I can't confirm it applied on 1 October 2025.

**Duties if the premises don't comply.** The provider must ensure rented premises comply with the rental minimum standards on or before the day the renter moves in [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The provider must also keep records sufficient to show compliance with s 65A [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) (the record-keeping duty for advertising, s 65E, also appears only in the later version [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)).

## Is the photo enough?

The documents don't say. They don't set an evidence standard or say how a Tribunal would weigh photos. Also, the mould standard covers mould "caused by or related to the building structure" [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf), so a photo shows mould but not necessarily its cause. The documents don't address whether a photo alone proves a breach.

- **Request urgent repairs.** If the premises don't meet the standards on or just after move-in, the renter may issue a request to the provider for urgent repairs [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

This applies whether or not the renter knew of the disrepair before moving in [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Ask for records.** The provider must keep records of compliance [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf), but the documents don't say a renter can demand them. The Director can require production of them [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

**Not covered by the documents:** the urgent repair timeframes, how to report an advertising breach to the Director, and penalties actually imposed.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I let a friend move into my rental without telling the agent. Now I want them out. What do I have to do?
answer:
**Short answer:** Under the Act, letting someone move in without the landlord's written consent can expose you to a notice to vacate. The documents don't set out a process for removing a friend who is living with you, so I can't tell you exactly what to do to get them out.

I've assumed you are the renter and the agent acts for the landlord. The law in force on 15 October 2026 is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 115 (dated 13 October 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Regulations, version 009 (30 June 2026), are also relevant [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

The Regulations summarise this the same way [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **The landlord can end the tenancy for this breach.** A landlord "may give a renter a notice to vacate rented premises if the renter has assigned or sub-let or purported to assign or sub-let the whole or any part of the premises without the residential rental provider's consent." The notice must give a termination date "not less than 14 days after the date on which the notice is given" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Notice requirements.** A notice to vacate is not valid unless it is in the prescribed form, addressed to the renter, signed, states the reasons, and states the termination date [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The prescribed form is Form 6 [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The documentary-evidence requirement in that section applies to other grounds, not to this one [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Consent cannot be unreasonably withheld.** A landlord "must not unreasonably withhold consent" to sub-letting, and an unconsented sub-letting is invalid unless the Tribunal decides consent is not required [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

2. **If consent is refused,** you can apply to VCAT for a determination that consent is not required. This applies only where the provider has withheld consent and you believe that is unreasonable [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **If the agent gives you a notice to vacate,** you can check it against the requirements above. Form 6 says you should seek advice immediately and lists community legal organisations on the Consumer Affairs Victoria website. The Consumer Affairs line is 1300 558 181 [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

- The documents do not describe how a renter removes an occupant, or what your friend's rights are if you ask them to leave.
- Whether your friend has any tenancy rights of their own is not addressed.

For the removal itself, you may need to rely on the friend leaving voluntarily or on a separate legal process. I can't confirm the steps for that from these documents, so please get specific advice from Consumer Affairs Victoria or a community legal centre.

question: It is 1 November 2019. I followed up repairs to leaking fixtures and got a notice to vacate the same day. I am renting month to month. What should I check if I think the notice is retaliation for asking for repairs?
answer:
**Short answer:** If your notice is a no-reason notice under s 263, the law says it is of no effect when it was given in response to your exercise of a right under the Act. You need to check which section the notice relies on and challenge it within 60 days.

**Which law applies:** On 1 November 2019, the closest version in the documents is the reprint dated 2 July 2019, which I'll call v088 based on its file name. The file name is the only source for that version number, since the excerpt doesn't state it. The v089 reprint is dated 4 December 2019, so it postdates your notice [[11]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)[[10]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf). The wording I could find for the key provision comes from the later v089 and v090 reprints, so confirm it against the v088 text before relying on it [[10]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf)[[12]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2020-02/97-109aa090%20authorised.pdf).

**What the law says:**
- A landlord can give a periodic tenant a notice to vacate without giving a reason under s 263. That notice must give at least 120 days' notice, unless a prescribed period applies [[10]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf).
- Under s 266(2), a s 263 notice "is of no effect if it was given in response to the exercise, or proposed exercise, by the tenant of a right under this Act" [[10]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf).
- Under s 266(3)(c), you cannot apply to the Tribunal challenging a s 263 notice after "the end of 60 days after the date on which the notice is given" [[10]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf). For a notice given on 1 November 2019, that is about 31 December 2019. Confirm the exact date.
- Repair rights include asking the landlord to repair. A tenant may apply to the Director about non-urgent repairs if the tenant has given the landlord written notice and the landlord hasn't repaired within 14 days [[11]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

**What to check:**
1. **The section cited.** If the notice relies on s 263 (no reason), the anti-retaliation bar in s 266(2) applies on its terms. If it cites a specific reason, such as repairs under s 255, I didn't find a retaliation bar for that section in the excerpts, so the argument is weaker.
2. **Timing and form.** Note the date you requested repairs and the date the notice was given. The notice must also meet the form and timing rules; I couldn't confirm those from the 2019 excerpts.
3. **Written evidence of the repair request.** Non-urgent repair applications require written notice to the landlord [[11]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). Whether an informal request counts as "exercising a right" is not addressed in the excerpts, so keep the written request and any reply.
4. **The 60-day deadline.** Calendar it from the date the notice was given.

**What you can do:**
- Apply to the Tribunal (VCAT) to challenge the notice within 60 days, as above [[10]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf).
- Collect your written repair requests, the notice, and any messages showing the timing.
- Get legal advice promptly. The documents don't cover how VCAT would decide a retaliation claim, and I can't tell from the excerpts whether the notice is valid.

**What the documents don't cover:** I couldn't find the v088 text of s 266 in the excerpts I retrieved, the prescribed notice period for periodic tenancies, or the VCAT procedure for these challenges in force on 1 November 2019.

question: It is 1 October 2025. I applied for a rental at the advertised price, then got an email saying I had withdrawn even though I had not. The property is now listed at a higher rent, and I heard someone else offered more than the advertised price. Can I challenge what happened, and what should I save as evidence?
answer:
**Short answer:** The law on 1 October 2025 prohibits rent bidding and a landlord or agent soliciting higher offers. It does not clearly cover a withdrawal email you never sent, and the documents don't set out how to challenge this or what evidence to keep.

**Which version applies:** For 1 October 2025, the latest retrieved version is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 110, incorporating amendments as at 6 August 2025 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Authorised Version No. 111 (as at 25 November 2025) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) and No. 115 (as at 13 October 2026) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) postdate your date, so I haven't relied on them for the law in force then.

**What the law says**

- **Advertised fixed rent:** A provider or agent must not advertise premises unless the rent is advertised or offered as a fixed amount [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **No soliciting higher offers:** A provider or agent "must not solicit or otherwise invite an offer of an amount of rent that is higher than the advertised amount of rent." The penalty is 60 penalty units for a natural person and 300 for a body corporate [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **No accepting unsolicited higher offers:** The version of section 30F(4) that prohibits accepting an unsolicited higher offer appears in Authorised Version No. 111 and was inserted by No. 6/2025 s.7 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). It does not appear in the Authorised Version No. 110 text I retrieved [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The documents don't give a commencement date for No. 6/2025, so I can't confirm this rule applied on 1 October 2025.
- **Misleading conduct:** A provider or agent must not induce a person to enter a residential rental agreement by misleading or deceptive conduct, and section 472(1A) provides for Tribunal orders for contraventions [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Section 30G also bars false or misleading advertising of rent [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Whether a withdrawal email you didn't send fits these sections depends on the facts, and the documents don't address it directly.

**What you can do or ask**

- **Challenge the conduct:** The documents show that misleading conduct under section 30E can lead to Tribunal orders under section 472(1A) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). They don't set out the steps, time limits or forms for a complaint about bidding under section 30F, or for disputing the withdrawal.
- **Compensation:** Section 210AA allows an application to the Tribunal for compensation, but only for loss from discrimination [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Hearsay about the higher offer:** Under the section 30F text, what matters is whether the provider solicited or accepted a higher offer [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The documents don't say how to prove this.

**Evidence to save:** The documents don't list specific evidence. From general practice, not from the documents, you could keep:
- The original advertisement showing the fixed rent and date (screenshot or saved page).
- Your application and all correspondence, including the withdrawal email with its full headers.
- Any messages where you were asked to offer more, or told about other offers.
- Records of the new listing and higher rent.

**What the documents don't cover:** The enforcement process, time limits, and whether the withdrawal email itself breaches the Act. For those, seek advice from Consumer Affairs Victoria or a tenancy legal service.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I sent the official request form to keep a dog in my apartment three weeks ago. The agent said no because the owner is allergic, but the owner hardly ever visits. Can they refuse?
answer:
**Short answer:** Based on the documents, the owner probably cannot refuse just because they are allergic and rarely visit, and the 14-day deadline may already have passed. Whether a refusal is "unreasonable" is not fully settled by the documents, though.

**What the law says**

- The governing version is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 115 (file dated 13 October 2026), which is in force for 15 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). I am identifying the version number from the document's file name, since the cover page was not in the retrieved text.
- A renter may keep a pet if the provider has consented in writing or the Tribunal (VCAT) has ordered it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The provider "must not unreasonably refuse to consent" to a pet [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The provider is taken to have consented unless, within 14 days after receiving the request, they apply to the Tribunal for an order that refusal is reasonable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- When deciding such an application, the Tribunal may consider the type of pet, the character of the premises, whether refusal is permitted under any other Act, and any other relevant matter. Allergy is not listed [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The Regulations' standard form also says the rental provider "must not unreasonably refuse a request to keep a pet" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

**Applying this to your situation**

- The agent's refusal is not, by itself, a Tribunal application. Under the 14-day rule, if the provider did not apply to VCAT within 14 days of your request, they are taken to have consented [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Your request was made about three weeks ago, so the 14 days have probably run out. You should confirm the exact date you sent the form and whether any VCAT application has been lodged.
- The documents do not define "unreasonably," and they do not say whether an owner's allergy is a reasonable ground for refusal. The listed Tribunal factors do not mention allergies [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The owner's rare visits are also not addressed in the documents.

**What you can do or ask**

1. Check the date you gave the request and the date of the agent's refusal.
2. Ask the provider or agent in writing whether they have applied to VCAT. If they have not within 14 days, you may treat the pet as consented to under the deemed-consent rule [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. If you are not sure whether the 14 days have run, or if the provider has applied, seek advice (for example, from Consumer Affairs Victoria or Victoria Legal Aid). The retrieved documents do not include their contact details.
4. Be aware of the risk on the other side. If the Tribunal later orders a pet excluded, the provider may give a notice to vacate if the order is not complied with after at least 14 days, with at least 28 days' notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**What the documents do not cover**

- Whether an owner's allergy counts as a reasonable ground for refusal.
- Any VCAT decisions on similar cases.
- The exact date your request was received.

question: It is 1 October 2025. Our landlord gave us a notice to vacate because they were selling. The buyer pulled out, but the landlord hasn't withdrawn the notice. Do we still have to leave?
answer:
**Short answer:** Based on the retrieved documents, the notice probably has not been withdrawn, so it still stands unless it is invalid or set aside. The documents do not say whether a sale-based notice lapses when the sale falls through, so get advice before assuming you must leave.

**Law in force on 1 October 2025:** The applicable document is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version v110, dated 6 August 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). A later version (v111, dated 25 November 2025) is not the law for 1 October 2025 [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

**What the law says**

- **Sale notices:** A landlord may give a notice to vacate if the premises are to be sold or offered for sale with vacant possession immediately after the termination date. If a contract of sale is conditional, the landlord may give the notice within 14 days after the last condition is satisfied. If the contract is not conditional, it must be given within 14 days after the contract is entered into. The termination date must be at least 60 days after the notice is given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Withdrawal:** A notice to vacate is withdrawn only if a notice of withdrawal is given. The withdrawal must be in writing and signed by the person who gave the notice and by the person to whom it was given [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The same wording appears in [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The retrieved v110 extract does not show this section, so check the full v110 text. On these documents, your landlord's failure to withdraw means the notice has not been withdrawn.
- **Form requirements:** A notice to vacate is not valid unless it is in the prescribed form, addressed to the renter, signed, states the reasons, is accompanied by the required documentary evidence, and states the termination date [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The v110 extract only refers to these requirements, so check the full text.
- **Challenging the notice:** For a sale notice, you may apply to VCAT challenging its validity within 30 days after the notice is given [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The retrieved v110 extract does not show this provision either.
- **Possession:** A landlord generally needs a VCAT possession order. Only Victoria Police can carry out a forced eviction, and only under a VCAT warrant [[9]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). Note that [[9]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf) is the Residential Tenancies Regulations, dated 25 November 2025, which is after 1 October 2025.

**What you can do or ask**

1. **Check the notice:** Confirm the date it was given, the termination date (at least 60 days after it was given under the v110 version), the prescribed form, the documentary evidence, and the stated reasons [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
2. **Diary the 30-day deadline:** If you want to challenge the notice, apply to VCAT within 30 days after it was given [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
3. **Ask the landlord in writing** whether they still intend to sell, and keep a record of their reply.
4. **Get advice promptly:** The Form 6 information sheet suggests contacting community legal organisations and Consumer Affairs Victoria on 1300 558 181 [[9]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
5. **Do not assume you can stay or must leave:** Only a withdrawal signed by both parties ends the notice, so any agreement to end it should be in that form [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**What the documents do not cover**

- Whether a sale-based notice remains valid after the buyer withdraws. Nothing in the retrieved documents addresses this.
- The full v110 text of the withdrawal, challenge, and re-letting provisions. The later version says a landlord who regains possession after a sale notice must not re-let the premises for 6 months, with penalties [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Confirm this applies under v110.
- Whether the 60-day minimum in v110 applies to your notice. The later version (v111) increased the sale-notice period to 90 days [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf), but the documents do not state how that change applies to notices given before it took effect.

question: It is 1 October 2025. My agent emailed to say the rent is going up. I tried to negotiate and they said no, but I never got an official rent increase notice. Do I have to pay the higher rent, and from when?
answer:
**The short answer:** On the documents I found, you probably don't have to pay the higher rent yet, because the agent has not given you a valid written notice. The law requires a formal notice, and it has to be given at least 60 days before the increase.

## What the law says (as at 1 October 2025)

The version of the Act in force on 1 October 2025 is the Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version v110, dated 6 August 2025 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The later version, v111 dated 25 November 2025, changes the notice period to 90 days, but it was not in force on your date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

- **Notice is required:** A rental provider must give the renter "at least 60 days notice in the prescribed form of a proposed rent increase" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Notice must contain specific details:** It must state the amount of the increase, the method used to calculate it, and your right to apply to the Director within 30 days [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Invalid increases:** "A rent increase in contravention of this section is invalid" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Fixed-term agreements:** The rent cannot rise before the term ends unless the agreement provides for a specified increase [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Frequency:** Rent cannot be increased at intervals of less than 12 months [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

The prescribed form is Form 5 in the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, dated 1 July 2025. It states: "A valid notice of a proposed rent increase is required for all rent increases" [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). It also requires the current rent, the new rent, the start date, and the method of calculation [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

## Do you have to pay, and from when?

- **Not on the facts you describe.** An agent's email saying the rent is going up, followed by a refused negotiation, does not appear to be a Form 5 notice. Without a valid notice, the increase appears to be invalid under s 44(5) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **If a valid notice is later given,** the increase cannot start until at least 60 days after the notice is given [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The start date must be stated on the form [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **If you receive a valid notice,** you can apply to the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria within 30 days of the notice to investigate whether the proposed rent is excessive [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). You can also apply to VCAT. Under Form 5, you "will need to pay the increased rent amount from the date provided on this notice unless VCAT decides otherwise" [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do or ask

1. **Ask the agent in writing for a Form 5 notice.** Note that the form's rental provider name "cannot be the agent's name" [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
2. **Keep a record** of the email and your negotiation.
3. **Check the date the notice is given.** If you receive a valid notice, your 30-day window to apply to the Director starts from that date [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
4. **Get free help** from Consumer Affairs Victoria at 1300 558 181 or renting@justice.vic.gov.au, or visit www.consumer.vic.gov.au/renting [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

The documents do not contain the exact wording of the agent's email, so I can't confirm whether it could count as notice. They also don't say whether your agreement is fixed-term or contains a rent-adjustment clause, which would affect the answer. This is general information from the Act and regulations, not legal advice.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All four points are covered: Form 5 is required ('the prescribed form is Form 5'), at least 60 days notice is stated, and next steps include asking the agent in writing for a Form 5 notice and applying to the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria. The hardest point is softened by 'probably' and 'appears' but still falls clearly one way: 'you probably don't have to pay the higher rent yet, because the agent has not given you a valid written notice' and 'Without a valid notice, the increase appears to be invalid under s 44(5)'.
