question: It is 1 March 2023. Most of the power points in my rental are on one circuit, and the breaker trips when we run the kettle and the heater together. Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs, and what can I ask for?
answer:
Based on the Victorian residential tenancy laws in force on 1 March 2023:

**Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs?**
No, the retrieved documents do not specify a minimum number of electrical circuits that a rental property must have. Instead, the law sets minimum safety standards for the *equipment* protecting those circuits. Under the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (S.R. No. 3/2021), all power outlets and lighting circuits in rented premises are required to be connected to a switchboard-type Circuit Breaker (complying with AS/NZS 3000) and a switchboard-type Residual Current Device (RCD) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). 

*Note on timing:* This specific circuit breaker and RCD minimum standard officially comes into force on **29 March 2023** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**What can you ask for?**
A tripping breaker when running two high-power appliances together indicates an overloaded circuit or a potential electrical fault. You can take the following steps based on the regulations:
1. **Request an inspection by a licensed electrician:** Your landlord is legally required to ensure that all electrical installations, appliances, and fittings are checked every 2 years by a licensed or registered electrician [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). A tripping breaker falls under this maintenance requirement and must be addressed by a suitably qualified person (a licensed electrician) [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Ask for the most recent electrical safety check record:** You have the right to request the date and details of the last electrical safety check in writing from your landlord [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). 
3. **Request confirmation on upcoming compliance:** Since the new mandatory circuit breaker and RCD rules take effect on 29 March 2023, you can ask your landlord to confirm whether your switchboard already meets these requirements or if upgrades are planned before that date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

must-mention.reason: Yes. Both points are covered: the answer says 'the retrieved documents do not specify a minimum number of electrical circuits', and it gives the next step 'You have the right to request the date and details of the last electrical safety check in writing from your landlord'.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer says "the retrieved documents do not specify a minimum number of electrical circuits" and that the circuit breaker and RCD standard "officially comes into force on 29 March 2023", so it neither sets a circuit minimum nor says the standard applies on 1 March 2023.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I live in a rooming house and the two washing machines are coin-operated. Are they allowed to charge us to use them?
answer:
Based on the law in force on 15 October 2026, specifically the ***Residential Tenancies Act 1997*** (Authorised Version v115 dated 13 October 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) and the ***Residential Tenancies (Rooming House Standards) Regulations 2023*** (Authorised Version v002 dated 1 December 2024) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf):

### What the law says
* **Mandatory provision of laundry facilities:** Rooming house operators are legally required to provide laundry facilities, including a washing machine in good working order, for every 12 or fewer residents based on the maximum capacity of the house [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf). 
* **Charging for services:** If a private rooming house operator charges you for services (which can include the use of laundry facilities), they must give you a separate schedule of those service amounts *before* you take up residency. If you use the services, they must also provide you with an itemised account showing your individual use [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
* **Government-subsidised houses:** If your rooming house is operated by Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency, they may impose a service charge for laundry facilities only if it is not possible to accurately measure individual use. In these cases, the charge cannot exceed the actual cost of providing the facility [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**Regarding coin-operated machines:** The retrieved documents do not contain specific rules explicitly permitting or prohibiting "coin-operated" payment methods for private rooming house operators. However, because the law requires the operator to provide a washing machine as a standard amenity [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf), any charges for its use must be transparent and comply with the service charge rules outlined above [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### What you can do or ask
* **Ask for the schedule of services:** Request a copy of the schedule of services that was provided to you before you moved in, which should list any costs associated with using the laundry facilities [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
* **Request an itemised account:** If you are charged per use, ask for an itemised account showing your individual usage of the machines [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
* **Check the condition of the machine:** Ensure the washing machine is kept in good working order, as this is a mandatory standard for rooming houses [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf).
* **Verify the operator type:** If you live in government-subsidised accommodation, confirm that any service charge imposed does not exceed the actual cost of providing the laundry facility and that you received written notice of its imposition or any changes to it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

question: It is 1 October 2025. The photos in a rental ad look like they show mould in one of the bedrooms. Are they allowed to advertise it like that, and is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?
answer:
Based on the Victorian residential tenancy laws in force on **1 October 2025**, here is how the rules apply to your situation:

### 1. Are they allowed to advertise it like that?
**No.** Under section 65B of the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (No. 109 of 1997), a residential rental provider or their agent **must not advertise or otherwise offer premises to let** unless, at the time of advertising, they "reasonably believe the premises comply with the rental minimum standards" [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). If the photo genuinely shows mould that breaches the minimum standards, advertising it would be a direct violation of this rule.

### 2. What is the actual legal standard for mould?
Under clause 8 of Schedule 4 to the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (S.R. No. 3/2021), the law specifically requires that **"Each room in the rented premises must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure"** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). 
*(Note: This standard applies strictly to structural defects, such as leaks or poor construction. It does not cover mould caused by a tenant's daily activities like cooking or showering without adequate ventilation.)*

### 3. Is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the standards?
The retrieved documents **do not state** that a single advertisement photo is automatically sufficient proof that a property fails to meet minimum standards. While photos are explicitly permitted and encouraged in condition reports to document the state of the premises for potential disputes [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf), there is no rule stating an ad photo alone constitutes definitive proof of non-compliance. 

However, the law does require providers to keep records sufficient to demonstrate compliance with these standards [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Furthermore, when providing information to rental applicants, providers must disclose if they have received a repair notice for structural mould or damp in the premises within the last 3 years [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

### 4. What can you do or ask?
*   **Ask for proof of compliance:** Before signing an agreement, you can request that the provider show you records or evidence demonstrating that the property meets the rental minimum standards [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
*   **Document upon moving in:** If you decide to rent the place, take your own dated photos and complete a condition report immediately upon moving in to document the state of the bedrooms [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
*   **Request urgent repairs if structural:** If you move in and discover mould caused by the building structure, you have the right to issue a formal request to the provider for urgent repairs to bring the premises into compliance with the standards [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are present: the mould standard is quoted ('free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure'); the hardest point, that a photo alone is not proof, is covered by 'there is no rule stating an ad photo alone constitutes definitive proof of non-compliance'; and next steps are given, such as asking for proof of compliance and requesting urgent repairs after moving in.

question: It is 1 November 2019. I followed up repairs to leaking fixtures and got a notice to vacate the same day. I am renting month to month. What should I check if I think the notice is retaliation for asking for repairs?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997** (Vic), **Authorised Version No. 088** (dated 2 July 2019) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf), and the standard tenancy regulations, here is what the law says and what you should check:

### What the Law Says
Under Victorian tenancy law, a notice to vacate may be of no effect if it was given in response to the exercise or proposed exercise of a right under the Act [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). Additionally, rental providers have a legal duty to carry out non-urgent repairs (such as leaking fixtures) in a reasonable time after being notified [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). 

The standard Notice to Vacate form explicitly states that you may challenge the notice at VCAT if you believe it was given because you tried to exercise your rights as a renter [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

### What You Should Check
1. **The Stated Reason on the Form:** Review the "Reason for notice" section on your Notice to Vacate to see what grounds the provider has claimed, and compare this with the actual facts of your situation [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf), [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). 
2. **The Timeline of Events:** Document exactly when you requested the repairs and when you received the notice. Receiving a notice shortly after asking for repairs can be key evidence that it was given in response to you exercising your rights [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf), [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
3. **The Minimum Notice Period:** Verify that the termination date on the notice allows for the minimum number of days' notice required by law for the specific reason stated [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
4. **VCAT Challenge Deadlines:** If you believe the notice is retaliatory (i.e., because you tried to exercise your rights), you can challenge it at VCAT [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). You should seek advice immediately, and if the notice is for a fixed-term agreement ending, you generally have 14 days after receiving it to apply to VCAT [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

question: It is 1 October 2025. I applied for a rental at the advertised price, then got an email saying I had withdrawn even though I had not. The property is now listed at a higher rent, and I heard someone else offered more than the advertised price. Can I challenge what happened, and what should I save as evidence?
answer:
Based on the law in force on **1 October 2025**, your situation is governed by the ***Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (Vic), Authorised Version No. 110** (updated 6 August 2025) [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). 

### What the Law Says
Under Victorian law, rental bidding and auctions are strictly prohibited. The property must be advertised at a fixed rent amount [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). It is an offence for a rental provider or their agent to solicit or invite an offer of rent higher than the advertised amount, and they must not accept any unsolicited offers above that price [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). 

Additionally, making a false or misleading representation regarding the rent (or the status of an application) is prohibited under Section 30G [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Sending you a false email claiming your application was withdrawn to manipulate the outcome could also constitute misleading or deceptive conduct under Section 30E [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

### What You Can Do
Yes, you can challenge what happened. 
* **Apply to VCAT:** You can apply to the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT) for orders regarding these contraventions, as provided for under Section 472(1A) of the Act [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). 
* **Complain to Consumer Affairs Victoria:** You can lodge a formal complaint with Consumer Affairs Victoria, which has the power to investigate breaches of tenancy laws and issue penalties.

### Evidence to Save
To support your challenge at VCAT or with Consumer Affairs Victoria, you should immediately preserve:
* **The original advertisement:** Screenshots or links showing the property was advertised at the fixed price you applied for.
* **The false "withdrawn" email:** Save the full email thread exactly as received, along with any replies you sent denying the withdrawal.
* **Proof of your application:** Confirmation emails, submission timestamps, or receipts proving you applied at the advertised price and did not withdraw it.
* **Evidence of the new listing:** Screenshots showing the property re-listed at a higher rent.
* **Details of the higher offer:** If the agent mentioned another person's offer, save those messages or notes from phone calls (including dates, times, and who you spoke to).

question: It is 15 October 2026. I sent the official request form to keep a dog in my apartment three weeks ago. The agent said no because the owner is allergic, but the owner hardly ever visits. Can they refuse?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Vic)** as it stood on 15 October 2026 (Authorised Version v115, dated 13 October 2026), here is how the law applies to your situation:

**Can they refuse?**
No, the owner or agent cannot simply say "no" outright. Under section 71C(1), a residential rental provider **must not unreasonably refuse** consent to you keeping a pet [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf). 

**The 14-Day Rule (Your Key Advantage)**
Because you sent your official request form three weeks ago (21 days ago), the owner/agent has likely already missed their legal deadline. 
*   If the owner or agent wants to refuse your request, they **must apply to the Tribunal (VCAT) within 14 days** of receiving your request [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2020-02/97-109aa090%20authorised.pdf). 
*   If they do not apply to the Tribunal within those 14 days, the law states they are **taken to have consented** to you keeping the pet [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 

Since it has been three weeks and they just verbally said "no" without mentioning a Tribunal application, they are legally deemed to have given their consent.

**What if they *did* apply to the Tribunal?**
If they did apply to the Tribunal within that 14-day window, the Tribunal would then decide whether it is reasonable for them to refuse. In making this decision, the Tribunal can consider factors such as:

question: It is 1 October 2025. Our landlord gave us a notice to vacate because they were selling. The buyer pulled out, but the landlord hasn't withdrawn the notice. Do we still have to leave?
answer:
Based on the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (Vic) and the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (Vic) as they stood on **1 October 2025** (specifically the Authorised Version v110 dated 6 August 2025 [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)), here is how the law applies to your situation:

### 🔑 Direct Answer
**Yes, you are still legally required to vacate by the termination date specified in the original notice.** The fact that the buyer pulled out does not automatically cancel or invalidate the notice. A notice to vacate remains legally binding until its termination date expires, unless it is formally withdrawn by your landlord or set aside by the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT).

### 📜 Why the Notice Remains Valid
When a landlord gives a notice to vacate because they intend to sell the property, the law looks at whether the landlord genuinely intended to sell *at the time the notice was issued*. If that intention existed when the notice was given, and the notice met the statutory requirements (such as providing at least 60 days' notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2020-02/97-109aa090%20authorised.pdf)), it is valid. A subsequent change of heart or a failed sale does not retroactively void the notice.

### 📝 How a Notice Can Be Withdrawn
Under Victorian law, a landlord cannot simply tell you verbally that the notice is "off." It can only be withdrawn if a formal **notice of withdrawal** is provided [[13]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa098%20authorised.pdf). This withdrawal notice must meet three strict requirements:
1. It must be **in writing**;
2. It must be **signed by the landlord** (the person who gave the original notice); and
3. It must be **signed by you** (the tenant to whom the notice was given) [[13]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa098%20authorised.pdf).

If your landlord has not provided a document that meets all three of these criteria, the original notice to vacate is still in full force.

### 🛠️ What You Can Do
You have a few practical and legal options to handle this situation:

* **Request a Formal Withdrawal:** Ask your landlord to sign a written notice of withdrawal that satisfies the three requirements above. If they agree, you can legally stay in the property.
* **Negotiate an Extension:** Even if the landlord refuses to withdraw the notice, you can ask them for more time to find a new place. They are not legally obligated to grant this, but many landlords will agree to a short extension out of goodwill.
* **Challenge the Notice at VCAT:** If you believe the original notice was invalid (for example, it did not give the correct 60 days' notice, used the wrong form, or your landlord never genuinely intended to sell when they issued it), you can challenge its validity at VCAT [[13]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa098%20authorised.pdf). You must generally do this within **30 days** of receiving the notice, or before the hearing if the landlord applies for a possession order [[13]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa098%20authorised.pdf).
* **Ask for More Time at VCAT:** If your landlord applies to VCAT for a possession order because you haven't left by the termination date, you can still ask the Tribunal for additional time to vacate. VCAT will consider whether leaving immediately would cause you hardship and may grant an extension [[10]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

*Disclaimer: I am an AI assistant and this information is based on the retrieved statutory documents. Tenancy disputes can be complex; if your landlord proceeds with a possession order, seek immediate advice from a community legal centre or Victoria Legal Aid.*

question: It is 1 October 2025. My agent emailed to say the rent is going up. I tried to negotiate and they said no, but I never got an official rent increase notice. Do I have to pay the higher rent, and from when?
answer:
Based on the law in force on **1 October 2025**, here is how your situation is handled:

### Do you have to pay the higher rent?
**No.** Under Victorian tenancy law, a valid official notice is strictly required for all rent increases [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). An informal email from your agent does not count as a legally binding notice [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). Until a proper notice is served, you are only obligated to continue paying your current rent amount [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

### From when would the increase apply?
Because no valid notice was provided, there is **no lawful start date** for the increase. The rental provider cannot backdate or enforce a higher rent without following the correct legal process [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). 

### What the law requires (as of 1 October 2025)
According to the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (S.R. No. 3/2021), version v004, which was in effect on your query date [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf):
* **The correct form:** The rental provider must use the prescribed "Notice of Proposed Rent Increase to Renter of Rented Premises" (**Form 5**) to notify you of any increase [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). 
* **Notice period:** The provider must give you at least **60 days' notice** before the new rent applies [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
* **Required details:** The official notice must clearly state the current rent, the new rent amount, the start date, and the method used to calculate the increase (for example, the Consumer Price Index) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
* **Delivery method:** If the notice is sent by email, it is only valid if you have previously given explicit consent to receive tenancy notices electronically [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

### What you can do or ask
1. **Request the official Form 5:** Reply to your agent in writing and state that you have not received a valid Form 5 notice. Ask them to provide one immediately so you know exactly when the increase would legally start (which must be at least 60 days from the date they serve it) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
2. **Check your consent for email:** If you never agreed to receive tenancy notices via email, point out that their email cannot legally count as service of the notice [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
3. **Continue paying current rent:** Until a valid Form 5 is served and the 60-day period passes, you continue to pay your existing rent [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
4. **Challenge if necessary:** If they try to enforce the increase without a valid notice, you can apply to the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT) or contact Consumer Affairs Victoria for help [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

*(Note: The law was updated shortly after your query date in November 2025 to extend this notice period to 90 days, but the 60-day rule applies to your situation on 1 October 2025.)*

question: It is 1 October 2025. The photos in a rental ad look like they show mould in one of the bedrooms. Are they allowed to advertise it like that, and is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?
answer:

### **Can they advertise it like that?**
Under the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (No. 109 of 1997), version dated 6 August 2025 [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf), a rental provider or their agent is only permitted to advertise premises if they **reasonably believe** the property complies with the rental minimum standards at the time of advertising [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). If the provider knows or should know that structural mould exists, they cannot hold this reasonable belief. Advertising premises that do not comply with minimum standards without this reasonable belief is a criminal offence [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### **Is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?**
No, a single photo in an advertisement is not automatically sufficient proof of non-compliance for two key reasons:

1. **The specific cause of the mould matters:** The *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (S.R. No. 3/2021), version dated 1 July 2025, only require that rooms be free from mould and damp that is **"caused by or related to the building structure"** [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). A photo might show visible mould, but it does not prove whether the mould is structural (the landlord's responsibility) or caused by tenant activities like poor ventilation, lack of heating, or drying laundry indoors.
2. **Evidence standards:** The legislation requires rental providers to keep records sufficient to demonstrate compliance with minimum standards [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), but it does not state that an advertisement photo alone constitutes definitive legal proof of a breach. Proving non-compliance would typically require further evidence regarding the actual cause and extent of the mould at the time of advertising or occupation.

### **What you can do**
If you suspect the property has structural mould, you can request to see the premises in person before signing an agreement. If you move in and find structural mould, you can issue a written request to the provider for urgent repairs to bring the property into compliance with the minimum standards [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). If they fail to address it, you may apply to VCAT for an order requiring the repairs to be carried out [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

**3. Your right to request repairs**

question: It is 1 October 2025. I applied for a rental at the advertised price, then got an email saying I had withdrawn even though I had not. ### Can you challenge what happened?
**Yes.** The actions you described appear to breach several specific provisions of the Act:
* **Accepting higher offers:** A residential rental provider or their agent must not accept an unsolicited or uninvited offer of rent that is higher than the advertised amount [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). 
* **False advertising:** Providers and agents are prohibited from making false or misleading representations regarding the rent for a property [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
* **Misleading conduct:** It is illegal to induce a person to enter a residential rental agreement through conduct that is misleading, deceptive, or likely to mislead [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).

These actions are offences under the Act, carrying penalties of 60 penalty units for natural persons and 300 penalty units for body corporates [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). You can challenge this by lodging a complaint with Consumer Affairs Victoria (which investigates tenancy breaches) or by applying to the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT) or pursuing remedies under Australian Consumer Law [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf), [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

### What should you save as evidence?
While the legislation does not provide a specific checklist for this exact scenario, you must be able to prove the breach of the fixed rent advertising rules. You should immediately save:
* **The original advertisement:** Screenshots or links showing the property was advertised at a specific, fixed rent amount.
* **Your application records:** Emails, receipts, or portal confirmations proving you applied at the advertised price.
* **The false withdrawal email:** The exact email claiming you withdrew, along with any proof (e.g., sent emails from you) that you did not withdraw your application.
* **Proof of the new listing:** Screenshots of the property listed at a higher rent.
* **Evidence of the other offer:** Any communication or documentation showing another party offered more than the advertised price.

By preserving this evidence, you can demonstrate to Consumer Affairs Victoria or VCAT that the provider/agent solicited or accepted an offer above the advertised fixed amount and engaged in misleading conduct [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

question: It is 15 October 2026. I sent the official request form to keep a dog in my apartment three weeks ago. The agent said no because the owner is allergic, but the owner hardly ever visits. Can they refuse?
answer:
Based on the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (Vic), version **v115-2026-10-13**, which was in force on 15 October 2026 [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf):

### What the law says
Under section 71C(1), a residential rental provider (or their agent) **must not unreasonably refuse** your request to keep a pet [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). They cannot simply issue a blanket refusal and stop there. 

If they wish to enforce a refusal, they must apply to the Tribunal within **14 days** of receiving your official request form to prove that it is reasonable for them to do so [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If they fail to make this application within 14 days, the law automatically deems them to have consented to you keeping the pet [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

When deciding if a refusal is reasonable, the Tribunal will consider factors such as the type of pet and the nature of the premises, but it also has the discretion to consider **"any other matter the Tribunal considers relevant"** [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 

### What you can do
1. **Track the 14-day deadline:** Count 14 days from the day you sent your official request form. If the agent does not apply to the Tribunal within this window, you are legally deemed to have consent [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You can then keep the dog.
2. **Prepare for a Tribunal hearing (if they apply):** If the agent *does* apply to the Tribunal within 14 days, you will have the chance to contest the refusal. At the hearing, you should highlight that the owner "hardly ever visits" as a relevant matter under section 71E(2) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This demonstrates that the allergy poses little practical risk or interference in your day-to-day tenancy.
3. **Ask for clarification:** You can ask the agent to confirm whether they intend to apply to the Tribunal within the 14-day period, as a mere verbal refusal without a Tribunal application is not legally enforceable under the Act [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

question: It is 1 October 2025. Our landlord gave us a notice to vacate because they were selling. The buyer pulled out, but the landlord hasn't withdrawn the notice. Do we still have to leave?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Vic)** (v110, updated 6 August 2025) and the accompanying regulations in force on 1 October 2025, here is how the law applies to your situation:

### Do you still have to leave?
**Not automatically.** Even though the buyer pulled out, your landlord **cannot unilaterally cancel or withdraw the notice**. Under Victorian tenancy law, a notice to vacate can only be withdrawn if a written "notice of withdrawal" is signed by **both** the landlord (who gave the notice) and you (the tenant) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2020-02/97-109aa090%20authorised.pdf). 

Because you have not signed this document, the original notice remains legally valid. The collapse of the sale does not automatically invalidate it.

### What can you do?
Since the notice is still active, you have a few options:

1. **Negotiate with your landlord:** Because the buyer has withdrawn, your landlord no longer has an immediate need to sell the property with vacant possession. You could use this leverage to negotiate more time to find a new home or ask for financial compensation in exchange for voluntarily leaving.
2. **Wait for a VCAT application:** If you choose not to leave by the termination date, your landlord must apply to the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT) for a possession order [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). 
3. **Challenge the notice at VCAT:** You have the right to challenge the validity of the notice at a VCAT hearing (for example, if it was not given properly, or due to hardship) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). At the hearing, VCAT will decide whether your landlord was entitled to give the notice and will only make a possession order if they are satisfied that it is **"reasonable and proportionate"** to do so based on all the circumstances [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). 

### Recommended Next Steps
If you intend to stay or need help negotiating with your landlord, you should seek immediate advice from a community legal centre or contact Consumer Affairs Victoria at 1300 558 181 [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). They can provide specific guidance on how to respond to the notice and prepare for a potential VCAT hearing.

*(Note: This information is based on the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (Vic) and *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (Vic) as they stood on 1 October 2025.)*

question: It is 1 October 2025. My agent emailed to say the rent is going up. I tried to negotiate and they said no, but I never got an official rent increase notice. Do I have to pay the higher rent, and from when?
answer:
Based on the date you asked your question (1 October 2025), the relevant law in force is the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (S.R. No. 3/2021), Authorised Version v004** (effective from 1 July 2025) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). 

### What the law says about your situation
Under this version of the regulations, a valid notice of a proposed rent increase is required for all rent increases [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). Specifically:
* The rental provider must give you **at least 60 days' notice** of any rent increase [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
* The notice must be an official prescribed form (Form 5) that clearly states the calculation method, the new rent amount, and the start date [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
* Rental providers are prohibited from increasing the rent more than once every 12 months [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

Because you only received an informal email from your agent and never received an official notice, the higher rent is not legally enforceable. An agent's email or a refusal to negotiate does not satisfy the statutory requirement for a formal notice [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). *(Note: While later versions of the regulations increased this notice period to 90 days, the 60-day rule was still in force on your date of inquiry)* [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

### Do you have to pay the higher rent?
**No.** You are not required to pay the increased amount until a valid, official notice has been properly served to you [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). 

### From when would the increase apply?
If and when a valid notice is provided, the new rent can only take effect from the **start date specified in that notice**, which must be at least 60 days after the notice was given to you [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

### What you can do or ask
1. **Request the official notice:** Ask your agent to provide the formal "Notice of Proposed Rent Increase to Renter of Rented Premises" (Form 5) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). 
2. **Verify the details:** Ensure the notice includes the method used to calculate the increase and that the start date is at least 60 days away from when you received it [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
3. **Challenge if necessary:** If a valid notice is eventually provided and you believe the increase is excessive, you have the right to apply to the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria for a free investigation, or apply to VCAT to declare the amount excessive [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

question: It is 1 October 2025. The photos in a rental ad look like they show mould in one of the bedrooms. Are they allowed to advertise it like that, and is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?
answer:
Based on Victorian law as of **1 October 2025**, here is how the rules apply to your situation:

**1. Are they allowed to advertise it like that?**
No. Under section 65B of the ***Residential Tenancies Act 1997*** (Vic), Authorised Version No. 110 (dated 6 August 2025), a rental provider or their agent **must not advertise or otherwise offer premises to let unless at the time the premises are advertised, they reasonably believe the premises comply with the rental minimum standards** [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). If a rental ad explicitly shows mould, it strongly suggests the provider is failing this legal test of "reasonable belief."

**2. Is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?**
Not on its own. Under clause 8 of Schedule 4 in the ***Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*** (Vic), Authorised Version No. 4 (dated 1 July 2025), the specific minimum standard is that each room must be free from mould and damp **"caused by or related to the building structure"** [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). 

A photo alone is generally insufficient to prove a breach for two key reasons:
* **The cause matters:** The law specifically prohibits *structural* mould. Mould caused by tenant lifestyle factors (such as poor ventilation after showering) does not violate this standard, and a single photograph cannot prove the underlying cause of the dampness.
* **Proof relies on documentation:** To demonstrate compliance with these standards, rental providers are legally required to keep specific records [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). A single photo is considered circumstantial evidence rather than definitive proof of a structural defect.

If you suspect the property has structural mould, you would need further evidence (such as a professional building inspection or reports from previous tenants) to prove it breaches the minimum standards.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered. The answer states the standard that rooms must be free from mould and damp "caused by or related to the building structure". It says "A photo alone is generally insufficient to prove a breach". For the next step, the hardest point, it advises getting "further evidence (such as a professional building inspection or reports from previous tenants)", which is a reasonable step consistent with the law.

The section numbering (s 65B rather than s 65A) and the absence of s 91L do not bear on the version criteria.
